# Chemoattractant gradients guiding a cell toward a target

An immune cell hunting an infection site does not travel in a straight line by luck; it follows a chemical gradient, a signaling molecule released at the infection site that is most concentrated near the source and thins out with distance. The travelling cell reads the difference in concentration across its own two ends and steps toward whichever side reads slightly higher, over and over, closing the distance without ever needing to know where the source actually is in advance.

The signaling molecule itself is often nearly worthless as a resource, it carries no nutritional value and does nothing to fight the infection directly; its entire function is to be noticeable and to get weaker with distance in a reliable, readable way, so that a cell drawn in by a weak early signal keeps being drawn in by a slightly stronger one at every step, until it arrives somewhere genuinely useful to be. The gradient is a lure shaped like a trail, not a destination in itself, and the cell never sees the destination until it has already arrived.
